newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl visits Yeltsin to further NATO reform.
newsitem.headline: Kohl visits Yeltsin to further NATO reform.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl travels to meet Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Saturday hoping once more to use their close personal relationship to advance the cause of NATO expansion and partnership with Moscow.

Kohl last saw Yeltsin in September, shortly before the Russian president's heart surgery, and will now be the first Western leader to visit him since he returned to work in the Kremlin at the end of December.

One item is likely to dominate the agenda -- NATO's determination to admit members from eastern Europe while agreeing a special relationship with Russia in an effort to overcome Moscow's vehement objections to NATO enlargement.

"Because of the degree of trust it enjoys in Russia, Germany in some ways plays a a kind of role -- after close consultation with its allies -- as spokesman in Moscow for the Western powers," said Heinz Timmermann of the Federal Institute for Eastern Studies.

But other Western nations are also queueing to see Yeltsin after his recovery, with French President Jacques Chirac due in Moscow later this month and U.S. President Bill Clinton expected to meet the Russian leader in March.

Germany is easily Russia's biggest Western credit-donor, but much of the special relationship also depends on the personal chemistry between Kohl and Yeltsin, who have shared laughs in a sauna and boating in Siberia on Lake Baikal.

Russia has so far remained adamant it will not accept any eastward extension of NATO, which is widely expected to decide in principle at a mid-year summit to admit Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.

Last month Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov caused a stir in Brussels by declining a NATO offer to exchange military liasion officers and warned the West that plans to expand NATO would jeopardise arms control.
But German analysts say Russia has already reconciled itself to a first wave of enlargement and is taking a tough position in order to secure other concessions.
"Perhaps they might be looking for an effective veto on any further enlargement to the Baltic states or south-east Europe," said one Bonn foreign policy analyst, who declined to be named.
Similarly, Timmermann said, NATO might eventually agree that the Baltic states would not join NATO in the foreseeable future.
"Neither side is at all interested in a serious deterioration in relations," he said.

After divergent statements from Rodionov, Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and Moscow's Security Council secretary Ivan Rybkin, Kohl and the other leaders will be seeking assurances that Yeltsin's return means a more coordinated and predictable stance from Russia, Timmermann added.
Apart from NATO, Kohl may urge Yeltsin to push ahead with creating safer and more stable conditions to help overcome Western companies' continuing fears about investing in Russia.

Another perennial is the question of the repatriation of thousands of priceless works of art taken to Russia by the invading Red Army as booty at the end of World War Two. The issue has shadowed relations for several years and there has been little sign of movement.
